model.short: A recipe that turns what we know about a person (the features) into a guess about something we want to know (the target).
model.more: The three models in this activity were already fitted to the data. You explain how each one makes its guesses; you don't build or change the models.

feature.short: One piece of information the model uses, such as age, BMI or waist size.
feature.more: Each dataset has 4–10 features. The data dictionary on the Data & files page lists them with their units.

target.short: The value the model tries to predict: fasting glucose (mg/dL), systolic blood pressure (mmHg) or lung function, FEV₁ (mL).
target.more: Always show the target's units next to predictions so viewers know what the number means.

prediction.short: The model's guess of the target for one person.
prediction.more: A prediction is not a measurement. Comparing it with the person's observed value shows how far off the model is.

regression.short: Predicting a number (like blood pressure), rather than a category (like yes/no).
regression.more: All three models here are regression models: each predicts a number in the target's units.

training-data.short: The people the model learned from: 80% of each dataset.
training-data.more: Every row in the CSVs has a split column that says train or validation. A model usually looks better on its own training data than on new people.

validation-data.short: The other 20% of people. The models never learned from them, so they show how well a model does on new people.
validation-data.more: In boosting, we also use validation data to choose when to stop. Because we used it to make that choice, its error is slightly optimistic, so we call it a validation result, not a test result.

test-result.short: An error measured on data that was never used for any decision, including choosing when to stop. This activity has no separate test set.
test-result.more: So say "lowest validation error", not "test error", when you describe the stopping round.

residual.short: What's left over: the actual value minus the prediction. Positive means the model guessed too low.
residual.more: Example (illustrative): actual 130 mmHg, predicted 124 mmHg → residual +6 mmHg.

rmse.short: A typical size of the model's mistakes, in the target's units. Lower is better.
rmse.more: Square every residual, average them, then take the square root. Big mistakes count extra. Only compare RMSE within one dataset: 20 mg/dL and 20 mmHg are different things.

overfitting.short: When a model keeps getting better on its training data but worse on new people, because it is memorising noise.
overfitting.more: In boosting, overfitting shows up as training error still falling while validation error has stopped falling or is rising.

linear-regression.short: A model that predicts by adding up a fixed amount per unit of each feature, like a recipe of weights.
linear-regression.more: It draws the best straight-line (or flat-surface) fit through the training data. It can't bend, which is easy to explain and sometimes wrong.

coefficient.short: How much the prediction changes for one more unit of a feature, holding the other features fixed.
coefficient.more: Example (illustrative): a coefficient of +0.5 mmHg per year means two people who differ by 10 years of age, and nothing else, get predictions 5 mmHg apart. Coefficients have units, so you can't compare raw coefficients across features.

baseline.short: The prediction for the training average: the place every push starts from.
baseline.more: It is supplied as linear.baseline. It is not the intercept: the intercept is the prediction when every feature is 0 (age 0, BMI 0…), which describes nobody.

intercept.short: The prediction when every feature equals 0. Usually not meaningful, so don't use it as the starting point.
intercept.more: Starting point = intercept + Σ coefficient × training average.

contribution.short: How much one feature moves this person's prediction up or down from the starting point.
contribution.more: Push = coefficient × (this person's value − training average). Starting point + all pushes = prediction. A person who is exactly average on a feature gets a push of 0 from it.

importance.short: One person's biggest push only tells you about that person. A feature can push one person a lot and most people very little.
importance.more: For an "in general" comparison, use the typical effect (coefficient × standard deviation), not one person's pushes and not raw coefficients.

typical-effect.short: Coefficient × the feature's standard deviation: how much the prediction moves for a typical difference between people.
typical-effect.more: Supplied as linear.typical_effect_per_sd for numeric features. It puts features with different units on a fair footing.

reference-group.short: For a category such as ethnicity, the group the 0/1 columns are compared with. For blood pressure it is Non-Hispanic White.
reference-group.more: Pushes are still measured from the training average mix, so even the reference group gets a small push. Show sex and ethnicity as one menu each, not as separate on/off switches.

association.short: The models show patterns in survey data. They don't show what would happen if someone changed a value.
association.more: Say "people with higher BMI tend to have higher predictions", not "lowering your BMI would lower your blood pressure".

decision-tree.short: A model that asks a series of yes/no questions ("Is age ≤ 45?") and gives the average outcome of the training people who ended up in the same place.
decision-tree.more: Each final group is called a leaf. A tree's prediction can only take a few values, one per leaf, so its responses come in steps.

random-forest.short: Many decision trees, each a little different, whose guesses are averaged.
random-forest.more: The supplied forest has 100 trees. Its prediction is the average of all 100 tree guesses, so it always stays within the range of outcomes seen in training.

bootstrap.short: Each tree learns from its own random draw of the training people, picked with replacement, so some people appear twice and others not at all.
bootstrap.more: On average, each tree sees about 63% of the distinct training people. The supplied field bootstrap_unique_training_rows gives the exact count per tree.

feature-subset.short: At each question, a tree may only choose from a random handful of the features. This makes the trees differ even more.
feature-subset.more: The supplied forest tries √(number of features) at each split: 2 of 5 for glucose, 3 of 10 for blood pressure, 2 of 4 for lung function (field features_tried_per_split).

disagreement.short: How far apart the trees' guesses are for one person. It is not a confidence or prediction interval.
disagreement.more: Trees learned from overlapping data, so their spread isn't a calibrated measure of how wrong the forest might be. Call it disagreement between trees.

partial-forest.short: The average of only some of the trees, for example the first 10 of 100. Label it, so viewers don't mistake it for the forest's prediction.
partial-forest.more: Use the trees in their fixed, supplied order so everyone's running averages match.

gradient-boosting.short: A model built one small tree at a time. Each new tree corrects part of the errors left by the trees before it.
gradient-boosting.more: The supplied model has 500 rounds of depth-3 trees with learning rate 0.1. Round 0 is the training average.

round.short: One step of boosting: one new tree is added. After round m, the model has m trees.
round.more: Round 0 means no trees yet: every person gets the training average.

correction.short: What one new tree adds to (or subtracts from) a person's prediction in that round.
correction.more: Prediction after round m = prediction after round m−1 + correction m. The supplied corrections already include the learning rate, so don't multiply by it again.

learning-rate.short: How much of each new tree's suggestion is used, here 0.1 (10%). Small steps are slower but more careful.
learning-rate.more: A different learning rate needs a separately trained model. The optional 0.02 comparison is supplied; scaling the 0.1 numbers doesn't reproduce it.

stopping-round.short: How many rounds to keep. A good choice is near where validation error is lowest, not where training error is lowest.
stopping-round.more: Training error keeps falling as trees are added, even after the model has started fitting noise.

public-link.short: A web address anyone can open without signing in or asking for access.
public-link.more: Check by opening it in a private or incognito window.

github-backup.short: Your code saved in your GitHub repository. It only counts once you've pushed; saving on your laptop isn't enough.
github-backup.more: Commit and push whenever a section starts working, and again before you submit.

commit-sha.short: The unique code for one saved version of your repository, like 3f2c1ab….
commit-sha.more: Run git rev-parse HEAD, or copy it from the latest commit on your repository's GitHub page.

static-site.short: A website made only of files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, data) that the browser runs. GitHub Pages hosts static sites; it can't run Python.
static-site.more: The GitHub Pages starter is static: it reads the supplied JSON files in the browser.

model-outputs.short: JSON files with every number your app needs (predictions, pushes, tree guesses, boosting rounds), already computed and checked.
model-outputs.more: Use these instead of training models yourself, so every student explains the same models. Field guide: outputs/SCHEMA.md.
